## THE 3 HARD RULES

1. **Three touches maximum.** Touch 4 does not exist. MONITOR + 90-day recheck.
2. **One new asset per touch.** Repeating the same link is a reminder, and reminders are spam.
3. **Every touch logged.** Date, type, value, outcome — in T4.3 Followup-Tracker.csv.

CONFIDENTIAL OPERATOR ASSET — FREQUENCY DOMINION
"Your Electronic Press Kit is not a biographical brochure. It is an interactive single-screen Command Deck engineered to give a gatekeeper all critical operational facts in 20 seconds."
1. ARCHITECTURAL PHILOSOPHY & OBJECTIVE

Traditional independent artist press kits fail because they are designed for vanity rather than rapid gatekeeper evaluation. Music directors, festival booking managers, and sync supervisors receive hundreds of submissions every week. When confronted with a 14-page PDF or a cluttered website with five dropdown navigation menus, they immediately bounce.
The
One-Page EPK Command Deck
solves this by establishing a strict, single-screen responsive visual hierarchy. It answers the five core questions every gatekeeper asks within 20 seconds:
Who is this artist, and what is their visual authority?
(Block 1: Hero Identity)
What is their commercial sonic proposition in plain English?
(Block 2: 80-Word Bio)
What does the record sound like right now without friction?
(Block 3: Audio Deck)
Who else with institutional credibility has already validated them?
(Block 4: Proof Wall)
Where is their active regional ground game?
(Block 5: Tour Dates & Contact)
2. THE SIX-BLOCK MODULAR SPECIFICATION

rows.v: High-charisma landscape photo, artist title, genre tag, hometown city
Exactly 80 words; objective third-person tone; two verifiable career facts
15px-17px clean sans-serif; 1.5 line height; zero poetic fluff
Lead single at top + instant Broadcast Master WAV download button
HTML5 audio player; instantaneous playback; no login or download wall
Four verifiable receipt cards: station adds, editorial quotes, ticket counts
High-contrast badge styling; active hyperlinks to external proof
Chronological 90-day live schedule: Date, City, Venue, Capacity, Tickets
Tabular format; prominent highlight on upcoming regional dates
Direct mobile phone, direct email, booking & management contact
Click-to-call / click-to-email active links; zero generic forms

spans.v: 3. COPYWRITING FORMULA FOR THE 80-WORD BIO
Follow this strict three-sentence template:
Sentence 1 (Identity & Sonic Stance):
"[Artist Name] is a [City]-based [Genre] artist blending [Sonic Element A] with [Sonic Element B], delivering [Specific Emotional/Listener Feeling]."
Sentence 2 (Institutional & Broadcast Proof):

"Currently in rotation on [Station Callsign A] and [Station Callsign B], their latest single '[Track Title]' peaked at #[Chart Position] on [Relevant Chart] following sold-out showcases at [Notable Venue]."
Sentence 3 (Current Operational Milestone):
"With [Upcoming Tour Name] routing across [Region] this fall, [Artist Name] brings an uncompromising broadcast-ready sound to audiences and programmers alike."
4. DEPLOYMENT PROTOCOL & BEST PRACTICES
Host at a Dedicated URL:
Host your Command Deck at
artistname.com/epk
or
artistname.com/radio
. Never send an attached document.
Zero Password Barriers:
Never password-protect your press kit. A gatekeeper arriving from a pitch will immediately close the tab if blocked by a login.
Mobile Screen Optimization:
Ensure Blocks 1, 2, and 3 are 100% visible on a standard smartphone screen without horizontal scrolling.

compliance.source: Derived from Lesson 1.4 (No-Spam Oath), Heat-Map Directory Usage Rules, and the 3-Touch Follow-Up guide
principles: Three touches maximum per station per campaign. After touch three: silence, not a fourth email.
Never BCC a market. Every send is addressed to a named human at one station.
Verify the contact before sending; never invent a name, role, or claim of familiarity.
A stop is permanent: honor opt-outs, 'remove me' replies, and different-instruction replies by suppressing the contact for this release cycle onward.
Never attach heavy files cold; offer links and send assets only on request (keeps you off blacklist triggers).
Numbers in pitches must be your own verifiable metrics — no invented streams, sold-out claims, or 'everyone is talking about' language.
One play is a spin, not rotation. Report outcomes exactly as verified; never imply ongoing support from a single add.
No payola, no disguised sponsorship, no undisclosed consideration for airplay — federal law (US 47 U.S.C. § 317) and basic respect.
Give the station a story it can tell its own listeners; local context is the service you provide.
Thank-you protocol is non-transactional: gratitude for adds/ints carries no ask attached.

decoder.title: HOW RADIO IS ACTUALLY MEASURED (THE RATINGS ENGINE)

spans.v: Every commercial station is fighting for one currency:
listenership
, measured by Nielsen Audio.
PPM markets (≈ top 48 metros):
people wear a Portable People Meter that logs listening
minute by minute

— every quarter-hour, every daypart, every station change. PPM stations have real data on exactly when their audience spikes. This is why drive-time and daypart fit matter so much: a station knows precisely which slots have the ears.
Diary markets (the rest of the country):
listeners write down what they heard in a diary. Coarser, moodier, and influenced by how memorable a station is. In diary markets, a song's
catchiness and station branding
matter disproportionately — because a listener has to
remember
to write your station down.
"The book" / book periods:
ratings are delivered in quarterly "books" (PPM markets get monthly data). Stations run "ratings weeks" — typically the
last two weeks of each book period
— when programming gets conservative: fewer risks, more proven hits. Believing you can break an unknown during a ratings week is amateur thinking. Launch around book starts, not book ends.
The metrics that matter to a PD:
cume
(how many unique people heard the station) and
AQH

(average quarter-hour audience). Songs are inventory that either grows cume (a hit brings new listeners) or holds AQH (a familiar track keeps people from tuning away). Your pitch should answer one of those two jobs — not "this song is good."
Insider translation:
the PD's yes is a ratings bet. The format, the clock, and the slot matter more than your artistry. Serve the bet and you win the slot.

decoder.title: THE CLOCK — HOW AN HOUR IS REALLY BUILT

spans.v: Every hour of radio is a
clock
: a fixed skeleton of intros, current hits, recurrents, golds, local breaks, sweepers, and legal IDs. A PD literally has a printed clock sheet.
The rotation categories (record pools that a song lives in):
What this means for you:
you don't need to be a power record to win — you need to be
a current

. The fastest win for an unknown is a specialty slot (night, weekend, local-focus), then get upgraded from specialty to medium by proving reaction. That ladder — specialty → medium → power — is the industry's actual entry ramp, and it's almost never explained because the artists who know it don't share it.
Insider move:
when a PD says "it's in light rotation," that's not a no — that's a category. Your job becomes a
rotation upgrade
, which is a much smaller ask: send listener-feedback receipts, ticket data, and stream spikes until the song graduates.

decoder.title: ADD CYCLES — WHEN STATIONS ACTUALLY SAY YES

spans.v: Radio doesn't decide daily. It decides on
cycles
Commercial stations:
most formats have set "add dates" — often
Tuesdays
(matches new-music Tuesday and the industry's weekly cadence), though formats differ (some add Monday, some Friday, country historically Tuesday). The promo industry calls a record's big date an
"impact date."
Pitch timing is built around
the add day
, not around your release day.
College and community stations:
music directors add on their own
weekly cycles
during business hours. College rotation is refreshed
weekly
— which means a Friday pitch gets heard Monday, and a Monday pitch can make the next rotation list.
Ratings weeks:
the "no new music" window. Don't pitch an unknown into the last two weeks of a book unless you're already in rotation.
Insider move:
ask the question that unlocks the calendar:
"What's your add cycle — and what day does rotation news go out?"
You're not asking for airplay; you're asking for their operational schedule. That question alone separates you from 99% of emails, and the answer tells you exactly when to send.

decoder.title: THE COLLEGE RADIO MACHINE (THE BEST KEPT LANE)

spans.v: College radio is not "lesser" — it's the only radio format with
structural hunger
: DJs and music directors who actively want new music, weekly rotation updates, and measurable charts.
The charts are real, public, and trackable.
The
NACC 200
(North American College Chart) and
RMR

(Radio Monitor, the college airplay ranker) are the reporting lanes that labels and supervisors actually watch. Getting on the chart is how an unknown becomes "charting" — and "charting at college radio" is the single most undervalued proof line in independent music.
The rep-network shortcut:
college radio promotion is commonly run through
college rep networks
— teams of student and regional reps who pitch stations, track adds, and report spins for a weekly fee. Labels use them for a reason: college stations respond to
personal reps
far better than email.
Why it matters to you:
college adds are cheap, fast, and they
feed the NACC chart
, which is verifiable proof for the commercial pitch, the sync license, and the sponsor deck.
Insider move:

you don't need a rep network to get the first 10 adds — you need the heat map, the specialty hunt, and the weekly cycle. But once you're charting, a rep network can scale the lane — and that's exactly what the Empire Loop (Module 6) is built to feed.

decoder.title: HOW THE PROMOTION INDUSTRY ACTUALLY MOVES MUSIC

spans.v: The label promotion machine, in order:
Service the record
— send the music + one-page brief to the station list through delivery platforms or direct link. (This is your Module 3 payload.)
Adds campaign
— an independent promo rep (or label staff) works the list week after week: calls, emails, playlist check-ins, spin tracking. The rep's whole job is
adds and rotation upgrades.
Chart week
— every week, stations report plays to chart services (Mediabase for commercial; NACC/RMR for college). The rep aggregates, reports, and the record climbs or stalls.
Second wave
— once a record is charting, the rep pitches it to bigger stations
with evidence
: "charting at college, 40 stations, trending in [markets]." Proof converts cold lists into warm ones.
What this means for an independent:
you can run a
condensed version of this machine
solo — which is exactly what this course teaches. The code word for the whole system:
the Add → Chart → Cascade loop.
Labels pay $2,000–$10,000 per record for what you're about to run yourself.

spans.v: A PD's yes is a
ratings bet
, not a taste vote.
Serve the
clock
, not the ego — 3:00–3:45, hook inside 12 seconds, clean edit ready.
Specialty → medium → power
is the entry ladder. Never skip rungs.
Tuesday add cycles and weekly college cycles
are your scheduling spine.
Never pitch during ratings weeks
to a station that doesn't know you.
College
charting is proof
— NACC/RMR are real, public, and supervisors read them.
The industry moves music in
four phases: service → adds → chart → second wave.
Run all four.
Rotation categories are asks
: light → medium is a smaller, winnable battle than unknown → power.
Spins are merchandise
— every spin is a data point you can sell (sync, sponsorship, booking).
Labels pay for what you're building — the machine is the product.

THE TRUST ARCHITECTURE (WHY IDENTITY CONVERTS)
Every radio decision is a
trust negotiation
between the PD's judgment and their risk. The singer's identity — how you show up — is the interface. Three layers, in order:
Competence layer
— "this artist has a machine." Proof stacks, EPK, audio package, named files, a professional signature. Competence is what removes the
friction
of saying yes.
Character layer
— "this artist is easy to work with." Polished follow-ups, promised deliveries kept, no guilt language, respect for the clock. Character is what makes a PD
want
to re-add you next cycle.
Contribution layer
— "this artist gives before asking." Assets, receipts, shout-outs, tickets, station IDs. Contribution is what turns an add into an ally.

Amateurs reverse the order: they ask first, promise competence only in the bio, and contribute never. The entire Module 1 is built to stack these three layers in the right order — because a PD who experiences you in reverse reads you as a transaction, not a partner.
THE UNHEARD TAX AS A COST MODEL (RUN THE ACTUAL MATH)
The Unheard Tax isn't a metaphor — model it like a business expense:
Opportunity cost:
one verified add per market per quarter ≈ 4 add receipts that can convert 2–3 placement/sponsor conversations. Zero adds = zero verifiable demand = those conversations don't happen.
Compounding interest:
every add is an asset that
keeps earning
: it feeds the proof stack, the NACC/RMR chart trajectory, the media kit, and the next pitch. The artist with 12 adds a year is not 12% ahead — they're on a different growth curve.
The decay cost:
every month of silence trains your audience, the market, and your own habits into "not a radio artist." Silence is not neutral — it's negative compounding.
Operator move:

put a dollar figure on it (your average ticket × your conversion rate × 52 weeks). That number is the only thing that makes you act at 11pm when you're tired. Motivation is a mood; a tax invoice is a system.
THE PROOF-STACK GRADING SYSTEM (USED BY PEOPLE WHO SCREEN ARTISTS)
Screeners rank proof in five buckets. Grade yours and fix the weakest:

rows.v: Other stations' spins, chart listings (NACC/RMR), label/industry co-signs
Verified press, real playlists, notable sync/placement
Streams, saves, ticket counts, live receipts
Unverifiable logos, paid features, fan screenshots

spans.v: The secret:

your goal is never a perfect stack — it's one S-tier receipt per market and two A-tier receipts. One spin at the right station is worth 10k streams. Target receipts by market, not by size. (This is why Module 2's heat map matters: it finds where your S-tier is achievable.)
THE NO-SPAM OATH AS A COMPETITIVE MOAT
The oath isn't virtue — it's scarcity engineering. 95% of artists are spam. When you send one precise, proof-loaded, personalized payload, you are
the
anomaly. The radio industry's inbox is so full of garbage that a clean, courteous, three-touch professional stands out more than the loudest record. The oath is your positioning. Treat it like one.
THE IDENTITY SHIFT EXERCISE (DO THIS AT 3 LEVELS)
Language:
audit every sentence for 7 days. Kill "please," "I hope," "just," "sorry to bother." Replace with the supplier frame: "Here's what this can do for your afternoon block."
Artifacts:
your signature block, email address, EPK, file naming, folder names — every artifact either says "hobby" or "operation." Rename everything this week.
Calendar:
operators have a Monday operating memo and a quarterly audit. Add both to your calendar right now. Identity is schedule, not mood.
THE ONE SECRET MOST ARTISTS NEVER LEARN
PDs remember how you made them feel when they said yes — not how good your song was.
The thank-you, the receipts, the no-pressure follow-ups, and the second-release check-in are what turn a one-time slot into a standing relationship. Identity is not the pitch. Identity is the
aftermath

THE MARKET-TIER SYSTEM (STOP SORTING STATIONS — SORT MARKETS)
Stations don't exist in a vacuum — they live in
market tiers
with different physics. Target by tier, not by size:

rows.v: Hunger for new music, weekly cycles, chart-able
Add cycles exist, ratings pressure moderate

spans.v: The classic label move:
college-town campaign → chart → mid-metro add → PPM-metro pitch with the chart.
You can't skip tiers and expect breaks. The heat map should be tier-tagged, not just ring-tagged.
CHEAT CODE 1 — THE SPECIALTY-SHOW HUNT
The highest-acceptance inventory in radio isn't a format — it's a
show
. Specialty shows (late-night, genre, regional, themed, new-music blocks) have hosts who
need
to fill time and
love discovering
. Find them through:
Station "shows" / "programs" pages (almost every station lists specialty shows with host names).
NACC and RMR charts (charting stations have genre-specific shows — see who's charting adjacent artists).
Instagram/DM direct to hosts (specialty hosts are contactable; MDs are gate-kept).
Show descriptions: "local focus," "new music," "undiscovered," "hip-hop showcase," "indie hour" — those are acceptance signals.
Rule:
one specialty-show add per week is a faster path to a 10-add year than 200 emails to commercial MDs. Week one of every campaign: hunt 10 specialty hosts in your tier-1 markers.
CHEAT CODE 2 — THE FORMAT-INTELLIGENCE RADAR
A station's website says one thing; its playlist says everything. Before scoring any station:
Pull the
last 10–15 songs
(website "recently played," online stream history, or the station's socials).
Log tempo, energy, era mix, and genre drift — is it "alt but plays pop?" "country but plays rock crossover?"
Check the specialty shows
— a station might
look
closed but host a local show that's wide open.
Compare against your track. Judge the gap, not the label.
Format scores without playlist reality are fiction. The 12-point check exists to stop you from pitching the station's
brand
instead of its
clock
CHEAT CODE 3 — WHO ACTUALLY DECIDES (THE CONTACT TRIAGE)
Different stations, different deciders:
Commercial:
MD (music director) for adds; PD for rotation upgrades; APD sometimes. Start at MD; escalate politely.
College:
music director (often several, per genre) — the
genre MD
is the real target, not the station's general email.
Community/specialty hosts:
the
host
decides the show; the MD decides the station. Pitch the host for the show, then use the show as a route into the station.
Online:
the founder/owner is usually the decider and the most responsive human in radio.
Insider move:
a station's "music director" receives 100+ emails. A station's
genre-specific MD
receives 12. Find the genre MD. This one change alone can triple your reply rate.
CHEAT CODE 4 — THE 20-STATION ALLOCATION FORMULA
Don't fill your war room 20 random stations. Allocate for outcomes:
10 slot-
(specialty + college, high acceptance, proof-producing)
6 ladder shops
(stations that can upgrade you from specialty to rotation)
3 market-makers
(the one or two commercial stations that matter in each metro)
1 wildcard
(a stretch station with an actual human path)
This allocation is why 5 adds in 21 days is achievable: 10 high-acceptance slots aren't a hope, they're a probability.
CHEAT CODE 5 — THE PRE-ROLL FIRE TEST
Before any tour-date campaign: verify the market is
actually

reachable — drive time, venue capacity, station density, and whether any of your 10 slot stations have a local show that can plug the date. A date with zero station density is a concert, not a campaign. Fire the pre-roll only where the map says yes.
THE ONE SECRET MOST ARTISTS NEVER LEARN
The best 20 stations are not the ones that play your genre — they're the ones that play your

neighborhood* of the genre.** A station that plays 1980s college rock and a station that plays "indie pop but heavier" both say "alt" and both are wrong for you. The playlist radar catches the neighborhood. Format family beats format label, every time.

THE FOUR-SECOND STACK (THE ACTUAL ATTENTION ECONOMY)
A PD's evaluation isn't a read — it's a
stack of four-second decisions
Inbox preview (4s)
— subject line + sender + first line. If the subject is vague, dead.
Body scan (4s)
— "who is this, is there a receipt, what's the ask?" If the proof isn't in the first 20 words, dead.
Asset sample (4s)
— one click: is the audio playable in 60 seconds? If it needs a player, a login, or a download, dead.
Ask decision (4s)
— is the request yes-able in one sentence? If the ask is a list, dead.
Design every payload to win all four stacks before the PD has to
think
. That's what the 90-word pitch, the one-page EPK, and the 3-file audio package are for. The weapon isn't the pitch — it's the
zero-thought path to a yes.
THE DOMAIN & DELIVERY PROTOCOL (THE HIDDEN CREDIBILITY SIGNAL)
Decision-makers evaluate the
sender
, not just the message:
Send from a real domain
, not gmail.com.
pitch@yourname.com
reads operator;
yourname99@gmail.com
reads bedroom. Domain + professional signature is the cheapest status signal in the game.
Never send a zip, a folder, or a Dropbox link that requires a click-through.
One link per payload. One attachment per payload (the 90-sec file). Everything else lives on the EPK page.
File naming is branding:
ARTIST-SONG-90SEC
ARTIST-SONG-CLEAN-WAV
ARTIST-EPK
. A PD forwarding your file forwards your professionalism.
Test the mobile path
— 80% of first opens happen on a phone. Open your own email on your phone and time it: how many seconds until the song is playing? If it's over 60, rework the payload.
THE PROOF-SHAPING TRICK (HOW LABELS FRAME RECEIPTS)
A receipt is a fact.
Framing is the weapon.
Same number, different command:
Raw:
"2,100 streams this month."
Framed:
"2,100 streams this month — [NUMBER] of them in [your station's metro], up [NUMBER]% since the radio adds."
Super-framed:
"[Sister station] added it last week and [metro] streams jumped [NUMBER]% — this is the track your audience is already showing up for."
Always include: the market, the trend, and the third-party source. A PD doesn't buy your number — they buy the
direction
of your number in
their
market.
THE TWO-EMAIL SYSTEM (THE INDUSTRY'S ACTUAL CADENCE)
Promo houses don't send one email per station. They run
two waves per cycle
Wave A — the service email:
subject + proof + ask (your 90-word pitch). Purpose: get the listen.
Wave B — the value email (48h later):
"here's the 90-sec promo built for your board" or "here's the listener-proof from [metro]." Purpose: get the add.
Wave B is where most adds actually land — and 90% of independents never send it because they think one email equals one campaign. The two-email system is the single highest-ROI change in this module.
THE SUBJECT-LINE MATH (BORROWED FROM DIRECT-RESPONSE)
4–7 words wins. Long subjects get truncated on mobile — and truncation kills the engine.
Personal names in subjects
lift opens on cold lists.
Numbers in subjects
lift opens on proof-led lists.
Format-show references
lift opens on specialty lists. Match the engine to the station type, or the open dies.
Never reuse a subject that failed twice.
Two failures = the angle is wrong for that list; change engines, not words.
Track everything in T3.1.
Your personal data of
your
market beats every general rule ever written.
THE AUDIO WEAPON: WHAT LABELS ACTUALLY SERVICE
The industry's service standard isn't "a song" — it's a
radio package
The 90-second promo
(hook + voice + CTA) — the
pitch
in audio form.
The radio edit
(clean, 3:00–3:45, hook < 12s) — the
inventory
The 30-second payload
(for IDs, beds, and the promo team) — the
derivative
that gets forwarded.
Produce all three before the first send. The hour you spend in the studio saves 20 hours of campaign repair — because a PD who has to ask "do you have a clean edit?" is a PD who hasn't added you yet.
THE ONE SECRET MOST ARTISTS NEVER LEARN
The reply you want is not "we'll play it." The reply you want is a question.
"Send the WAV," "what's the clean edit?" — that's the PD engaging with the
logistics
of saying yes, which means the decision is already 80% made. When you get a question, treat it as a
yes in progress
: answer within 4 hours with a phone number and a 12-minute call offer. This is the highest-leverage moment in the entire campaign and almost nobody recognizes it.

the campaign is a
weekly machine

Labels don't tell a station "this is out." They tell the station
"this is the impact date — play it the week of [date]."
That frames the add as a
scheduled event
, not a favor:

Your version:
give your campaign an internal impact date. Announce it in the pitch — "servicing [city] stations the week of [date]" — and time wave 1 exactly 1–2 weeks
before

on

THE COLLEGE CHART EXPRESS (SERVICE → ADDS → CHART → SECOND WAVE)
This is the mechanic the whole campaign optimizes for:

(wk 1): 10 college slots + 4 specialty — the Tier-1 allocation.
Adds
(wk 2): rotation boards pick up; you track adds daily in T4.4.
Chart
(wk 3): college stations report to NACC/RMR. Chart position is
evidence
Second wave

Run this loop and you're doing what labels pay $2,000+ per record for — with 20 stations and 21 days. The first add's real job is to start the chart. The chart's real job is to make the next 20 stations easy.
THE ROTATION-UPGRADE STRATEGY (THE KILLER FOLLOW-UP)
Most artists treat a light-rotation add as the end. Operators treat it as the
start of the upgrade campaign
Week after the add:
thank-you + listener-feedback receipts (streams, tickets, requests).
Two weeks after:
second receipt — usually market-specific ("your metro streams +30%").
Three weeks after:
the upgrade ask:
"Is there a path for [SONG] to move into medium? We can support with [asset]."
The upgrade ask is the single most winnable ask in the industry — it's a
category change
, not a new favor — and it's the one almost no independent ever makes.
THE SPIN-TRACKING DISCIPLINE (WHAT LABELS CHASE)
Spins are the industry's raw score. Track weekly per station:
adds
spins
rotation category
chart position
. The total spin count is your
momentum number

— the number that appears on the second-wave pitch, the sync package, the sponsor deck, and the booking email. Without weekly spin tracking, you're running a campaign without a scoreboard. With it, you're running a business.
THE 3-TOUCH ESCALATION PSYCHOLOGY (THE INSIDER VERSION)
Touch 1:
the ask lands. Silence = the PD is
not deciding yet
(busy, not hostile).
Touch 2 (value):
the receipt or asset gives them a
new reason
. This is where the "busy but interested" cohort converts.
Touch 3 (grace):
the close. Politeness + an open door. This is where the "I need a deadline" cohort converts — and where the "no" cohort converts into a
relationship
instead of a burn.
The system's secret: all three touches are about the
next campaign
too. Touch 3's grace close is what makes touch 1 of your next release warmer than touch 3 of this one.
THE ONE SECRET MOST ARTISTS NEVER LEARN
Adds happen in waves, not trickles.

If you see 2–3 adds land in one morning, the rest of the week's board is likely moving too — that's the rotation cycle turning. Watch the wave: when it turns, escalate the second-wave pitch to every station that
hasn't
added yet, with the fresh proof. Timing the second wave off the first wave's momentum is the difference between 5 adds and 11.

Radio relationships move in ladder rungs. Every interaction should climb one rung — never skip, never stall:

rows.v: Listen 3 min, one ask, one next step
Shares feedback, format info, goes to bat

spans.v: The ladder is why Module 5's cadence exists: a call doesn't get you a champion; the
year

THE THANK-YOU MATRIX (WHAT LABELS ACTUALLY DO FOR THEIR CHAMPIONS)
The gesture hierarchy, keyed to rung:
Rung 4 (add):
specific 3-day thank-you + social clip tagging the station.
Rung 5 (upgrade/repeat):
2-week asset (station ID, premiere, reserved tickets) + an on-air shout-out offer.
Rung 6 (champion):
90-day value drop —
no ask attached
. Introduce them to an artist. Send a listener for the request line. Give them the story first.
The matrix's rule:
the gesture is always one rung above the ask.

THE 12-MINUTE CALL: THE INSIDER SCRIPT QUEUE
Beyond the structure, the
sequence of questions
does the heavy lifting:
The warm-up is bait, not small talk.
"What's the most exciting thing that's happened on [show] this month?" Their answer is a gift: it tells you exactly what they're proud of — and what to reference forever after.
The format question is a market scan.
"What does a new record need to do to fit here?" The answer contains their internal criteria —
their wording
— which you can mirror in every future pitch.
The timing question is a calendar unlock.
"When's your add cycle and what day does rotation go out?" Answers set your next campaign's dates.
The ask is the smallest possible thing.
One slot. One show. One recheck date. The call's goal is the
next step
, not the commitment.
Golden rule:
never end a call without a next step and a date. No next step = no relationship. The 12-minute call that ends in a date becomes rung 3 → rung 4 in 72 hours.
THE INDUSTRY ETIQUETTE CODE (VIOLATIONS THAT BURN WELLS)
Never pitch another record in the same conversation as a thank-you.
The thank-you is its own message. Momentum is not a coupon.
Never ask a PD for a separate favor (press, playlist, social) in the same ask.
Radio owes you one thing per cycle. One ask, one cycle.
Never argue about a "no."
A "not now" is a calendar answer, not a judgment. A polite "understood, checking back in [month]" converts a no into a recheck — which is a win disguised as a rejection.
Never use the words "sorry to bother you" or "I know you're busy."
You're telling the PD their attention is a burden. They know. It's the ask that matters.
Never send a gift with an ask attached.
The gift is the message.
Never share another artist's private contact or a promo rep's list.
The industry is small; leaks travel fast and kill trust permanently.
THE BURNED-WELL TRIAGE (POINTERS FROM THE REPLAY)
Repair priority is return-on-effort, not guilt:
Highest ROI:
the well you
ghosted
(a promise unkept). One honest bridge can recover a full ally in a month.
High ROI:
the well you
spammed
(blasted, went quiet). 90-day cooling + clean signal + new value. Slow but recoverable.
Medium ROI:
the
clash
well (pitched a mismatch, argued). Only recover if the format changed or a new MD arrived — check the playlist first.
Low ROI:
the
value-debt
well (got a yes, gave nothing back). Recover via a genuine giving period — and this one actually
improves
you: it's a discipline lesson, not a repair.
Never re-pitch a well before its cooling period ends. Never re-pitch with the same angle. Two violations and the well is permanent.
THE INTRO-WEB MULTIPLIER (THE CONFIDANT MOVE)
The highest-value relationship move in the entire system:
introduce two of your contacts who benefit each other.
The PD gets a useful connection, you get network gravity, and the rung you climb is irrelevant — you become a
node of value
. Two intros a month builds a confidant network faster than fifty emails. When your next record drops, the intros you made are the credits you've banked.
THE ONE SECRET MOST ARTISTS NEVER LEARN
A PD's time is the only inventory they can't restock — and they notice who respects it.
The 12-minute call, the 3-touch stop, the one-ask rule, and the thank-you economy aren't politeness; they're a
demonstration

that you understand the inventory. That understanding is what makes a PD think of you when a specialty slot opens, a local spot opens, or a new-music hour needs a guest. The relationship isn't the ask. The relationship is the
respect for the clock

THE RELEASE CALENDAR AS AN INDUSTRY ASSET
The 12-week operation is also a
market-timing system
Q1 (Jan–Mar):
post-holiday open — new formats, fresh ears, cheapest attention. Best for a debut.

spring + summer booking cycle — release with tour dates pre-rolled (the ticket lane fires here).

fall push — the industry's biggest attention window for independent music. The breakout release lives here.

Three releases a year maps to three attention windows. The "one release per quarter" rhythm is actually
three campaigns in the three open windows
— and one closed-window quarter spent on proof and audit. That's the difference between a calendar and a hobby.
THE 90-DAY AUDIT AS A BUSINESS REVIEW (NOT A REPORT CARD)
The scorecard's real output is three decisions:
Kill / keep:
which lane or market is bleeding? The audit gives you permission to kill the weakest column without guilt — the weak column is the one
repairing
, not the one you're proud of.
Scale / hold:
which lane returned the best margin per hour? The audit says where the next campaign's hours go.
Ascension:
which gate did you pass? The gates (Operator → Dominant → Empire) are capacity-based, not ambition-based. The audit is the only honest referee.
The rule:
one surgical fix per quarter. The audit's weakest-column rule exists because a machine with five weak columns gets fixed
one column at a time
. Fixing all five at once is the mistake that keeps ambitious artists busy and broke.
THE ASCENSION FINANCE (WHAT SCALING ACTUALLY COSTS)
Operator (solo):
20 stations, ~6h/week. Cost: your time. Revenue: 1–2 lanes.
Dominant (with support):
3 releases/year, 20–40 stations per campaign, a VA (10–15h/week), 3 lanes. Cost: ~$500–$1,500/month. Revenue: the first real six-figure attempt.
Empire (campaign team):
a rollout manager + a rep network for the college lane, multi-market campaigns. Cost: ~$2,000–$5,000/month. Revenue: seven-figure-scale mechanics.
Scaling is a
purchase

, not a reward. You buy the VA when the audit says your bottleneck is available hours, not quality. You buy the rep network when the college chart lane is the highest-ROI path and your hands are full. The gates exist so you never buy scale before the machine has proven it converts.

The industry's most valuable artist is not the best musician — it's the one with the most
provable* demand.** Every door in the seven-figure world (sync, sponsor, booking, label, management) opens on evidence, and radio is the only demand engine an independent can build that produces
public, verifiable, third-party receipts
. The Empire Loop is not about radio for its own sake. It's about owning the one proof engine that scales to a $1M funnel — for $97 and 21 days of system.

THE DOCTRINE

Most artists treat radio like a favor they're hoping to collect. They buy a contact list, blast a generic email to 18,000 inboxes, and call it promotion. A list is not a strategy. A blast is not a campaign. And hoping is not a business model.
Frequency Dominion is the opposite operating system:
You do not ask for airplay. You own the frequency.
An owner does three things a beggar can never do:
He chooses his targets like a buyer, not a suitor.
Every station is a customer with a measurable need, a format, a clock, and a competition. You serve the need — or you don't touch the station.
He proves value before he asks for it.
Proof stacks, EPKs, and 90-second audio weapons mean the Program Director's first impression is
"this is already a professional"
— not
"another artist wants my time."
He runs campaigns, not emails.
21-day load sequences, 3-touch follow-ups, expansion loops, and 90-day audits. Systems compound. Emails don't.
THE AUTOPSY: WHY PRIOR MATERIAL FAILS
Let's be brutal. The old playbook — the contact vault, the "email everyone" advice, the 400-word pitch, the press-kit PDF nobody opens — is dogshit for one reason:
It sells the who but never teaches the how.
A list of 18,000 names with no targeting system is a spam cannon. You don't get airplay from it. You get burned wells, marked-as-spam flags, and a reputation you have to climb out of.
The 400-word pitch is read for four seconds. It's an essay in an era of a 90-word attention budget.
"Just be consistent" is not a system. Consistency without a load sequence, a first-send wave, and a 3-touch follow-up cadence is just noise at a higher volume.
No proof stack, no heat map, no format scoring, no expansion loop, no audit = no compounding. Without compounding, every single release restarts at zero.
Frequency Dominion replaces all of it.

This is not a contact dump. This is the command layer that turns the contacts you already own — and the stations you haven't reached yet — into a predictable, compounding airplay machine. If you have the RadioReach Vault, you now have the keys. If you don't, this system tells you exactly who to buy, what to ask for, and how to win it.
THE SEVEN LAWS OF FREQUENCY DOMINION
The Unheard Tax is real.
Every week without airplay costs you reach, revenue, and leverage. That tax is the enemy. This course is the audit.
A station is a customer, not a favor.
Serve the PD's clock. Win the format. Respect the market.
Proof precedes the pitch.
Never ask a stranger to take a risk on an unknown. Show the proof stack first.
Targets are architecture, not luck.
Hometown heat map → format score → 20-station war room → campaign. In that order. Every time.
The pitch is a weapon, not a message.
90 words. One hook. One ask. Radio-ready audio in the first email.
Follow-up is a system, not a feeling.
Three touches, spaced, escalated, polite. Persistence without the stench.
Empires compound.
Proof → adds → exposure → income → better proof → bigger stations. The loop is the business.
